_readme: The specimen pool. Each day the game picks 3 specimens from it.
clue: shown before the answer, so it must not give the age or the answer away.
added: the date (YYYY-MM-DD, UTC) the specimen joins the pool. Days before that date never use it.
Ages are in millions of years ago (Mya). ageRangeMya is the 'spot on' window.
image: path to the photo in assets/. photo: who took it, the licence, and the page it came from. Every photo must have one.
Safe to do: add new specimens with today's date or later, and fix typos or facts.
Never do (after launch): delete a specimen, change an id, or change an 'added' date. Past days would change.
Entries marked example: true were the first starter content. Every entry has a source link for checking its facts.
sharp: true shows the photo unpixelated while guessing (for phoneys that need detail to be fair).

specimens.name: Trilobite (Elrathia kingii)
specimens.clue: A small, ridged, bug-like shape pressed into dark grey shale.
specimens.foundIn: Wheeler Shale, House Range, Utah, USA
specimens.fact: One of the most common trilobite fossils in the world. Trilobites were sea animals related to insects and crabs, and they lasted for nearly 300 million years.

specimens.name: Ammonite (Dactylioceras commune)
specimens.clue: A tightly coiled, ribbed shell, about 7 cm across.
specimens.fact: Local legend said Saint Hilda turned Whitby's snakes to stone. Victorian sellers carved snake heads onto ammonites like this one and sold them as 'snakestones'.

specimens.name: Tyrannosaurus rex tooth
specimens.clue: A long, curved tooth with a smooth tip and a cracked, crumbly root.
specimens.fact: T. rex replaced its teeth throughout its life, which is why shed teeth are among the more common T. rex finds. This one is at the Museum of the Rockies in Montana.

specimens.name: Megalodon tooth (Otodus megalodon)
specimens.clue: A huge triangular tooth with fine serrations, as wide as a hand.
specimens.fact: Megalodon was a giant shark. Its teeth could grow up to about 18 cm long, and sharks shed thousands of teeth in a lifetime, so they turn up often.

specimens.name: Fly in Baltic amber
specimens.clue: A tiny fly trapped inside a polished lump of clear yellow resin.
specimens.fact: Amber is fossilised tree resin. Sticky resin trapped insects so quickly that some still show tiny hairs and wing veins.

specimens.name: Seed fern leaf (Neuropteris flexuosa)
specimens.clue: A row of fern-like leaflets printed on a slab of dark rock.
specimens.fact: It looks like a fern, but Neuropteris was a seed fern: a plant that made seeds instead of spores. Forests of plants like this became today's coal.

specimens.name: Woolly mammoth tooth
specimens.clue: A heavy, brick-sized block with ridged plates along its top.
specimens.fact: Woolly mammoths ground up tough grass with teeth like this one, made of ridged plates of enamel. Like elephants, they went through six sets of molars in a lifetime.

specimens.name: Manganese dendrites
specimens.clue: Delicate black branching fronds spread across pale limestone.
specimens.fact: Not a plant at all. Mineral-rich water seeped into cracks in the rock and left manganese oxide crystals that grew in branching, fern-like patterns.

specimens.name: Chambered nautilus shell
specimens.clue: A coiled shell cut in half, showing a spiral of chambers inside.
specimens.fact: Nautiluses are still alive today. Their shells look a lot like ammonites, which died out with the dinosaurs 66 million years ago.

photo.author: Eric A. Lazo-Wasem, Yale Peabody Museum

specimens.name: Fake trilobite in a 'nodule'
specimens.clue: A stone nodule split open, with a trilobite on each half.
specimens.foundIn: Bought from a rock and fossil seller
specimens.fact: Everything about this is fake: it isn't rock and it isn't a fossil. The whole thing was moulded to look like a natural nodule split open. Fakes like this, and much more convincing ones, are sold to collectors and tourists.

specimens.name: Beringer's 'lying stones'
specimens.clue: Three flat stones, each with a creature standing out on its surface.
specimens.foundIn: A hillside near Würzburg, Germany, in 1725
specimens.fact: Professor Johann Beringer published a book about these 'fossils'. They had been carved and planted by colleagues who wanted to embarrass him.

specimens.name: Archaeopteryx (Berlin specimen)
specimens.clue: A small skeleton with feathered wings and a long bony tail, spread across pale limestone.
specimens.fact: Half bird, half dinosaur: it had feathers and wings, but also teeth, clawed fingers and a long bony tail. For over a century it was thought to be the oldest known bird.

specimens.name: Sabre-toothed cat skull (Smilodon populator)
specimens.clue: A big cat's skull with two enormous, blade-like upper fangs.
specimens.fact: Not a tiger: Smilodon belonged to a separate, extinct branch of cats. Its name means 'scalpel tooth', and it was first named in 1842 from fossils found in Brazil.

specimens.name: Giant deer skeleton (Megaloceros giganteus)
specimens.clue: A deer skeleton taller than a person, with huge, flat, spreading antlers.
specimens.fact: Also called the Irish elk, though it wasn't an elk. Its antlers could span over 4 metres, the biggest of any known deer, and some survived until about 7,700 years ago.

specimens.name: Glyptodon (giant armadillo relative)
specimens.clue: A huge dome-shaped shell made of bony plates, as big as a small car.
specimens.fact: A giant relative of armadillos. Its fossils were first found in Uruguay in 1814, but early scientists mistook them for a giant ground sloth.

specimens.name: Fossil herring (Knightia)
specimens.clue: A small fish skeleton, every bone visible, on smooth pale stone.
specimens.fact: The most commonly dug-up fossil fish in the world, and the state fossil of Wyoming. It was related to modern herrings.

specimens.name: Bat (Palaeochiropteryx tupaiodon)
specimens.clue: A tiny skeleton with long finger bones folded at its sides, on orange-brown shale.
specimens.fact: Fossils from the Messel Pit are so well preserved that some of these early bats still show the outlines of their fur, ears and wing skin.

specimens.name: Nummulites (giant single-celled shells)
specimens.clue: A handful of flat, coin-shaped stone discs, from pea-sized to larger than a coin.
specimens.foundIn: Near Al Ain, United Arab Emirates
specimens.fact: Each 'coin' was the shell of a single-celled sea creature. Limestones packed with them are common around the Mediterranean, including in Egypt.

specimens.name: Microraptor (four-winged dinosaur)
specimens.clue: A crow-sized skeleton with a long tail and a faint halo of feathers around it.
specimens.fact: Microraptor had feathered wings on its arms and its legs, giving it four wings. It was a small relative of Velociraptor.

specimens.name: Heart urchin (Micraster decipiens)
specimens.clue: A heart-shaped stone with a five-pointed star pattern on top.
specimens.fact: A sea urchin that lived buried in the sea floor, drawing in water through the groove at the front of its shell.

specimens.name: Ammolite (Placenticeras ammonite shell)
specimens.clue: A polished oval of rainbow colours, set like a gemstone.
specimens.fact: This gemstone is a fossil: the rainbow layer is ammonite shell. It's one of the few gems made by living things, along with amber and pearl.

specimens.name: Ichthyosaurs (Stenopterygius)
specimens.clue: A dolphin-shaped skeleton outlined in dark rock, with a smaller one swimming below it.
specimens.fact: Ichthyosaurs were sea reptiles shaped like dolphins. One Stenopterygius fossil shows a mother that died giving birth, with her baby coming out tail-first, like a whale's.

specimens.name: 'Devil's toenail' oyster (Gryphaea arcuata)
specimens.clue: A thick, grey, curled-over shell about the size of a golf ball.
specimens.fact: People once carried these fossil oysters to ward off rheumatism. Their curled shape earned them the name 'devil's toenails'.

specimens.name: Petrified log
specimens.clue: A cross-section of a tree trunk that has turned into colourful stone.
specimens.foundIn: Petrified Forest National Park, Arizona, USA
specimens.fact: Minerals slowly replaced the wood, keeping the shape of the trunk and even its rings. The park in Arizona is named after its huge numbers of these logs.

specimens.name: Mesosaurus
specimens.clue: A slender reptile skeleton with a long tail and a narrow snout, on pale grey rock.
specimens.fact: A small reptile that lived in water, yet its fossils turn up in both southern Africa and South America. That was early evidence that the two continents were once joined.

specimens.name: Scale tree bark (Lepidodendron)
specimens.clue: Dark rock covered in neat, diamond-shaped scales, like snakeskin.
specimens.fact: Not snakeskin: it's bark from a scale tree, which could grow 50 metres tall. Swampy forests of them helped form much of the world's coal.

specimens.name: Tully monster (Tullimonstrum)
specimens.clue: A stone nodule split in two, with a strange cigar-shaped creature printed inside.
specimens.fact: Scientists still argue about what it was. It has been compared to molluscs, worms, arthropods and fish. It has only ever been found at Mazon Creek in Illinois.

specimens.name: Trilobite (Phacops)
specimens.clue: A rounded, bumpy, bug-like creature with big eyes made of many tiny lenses.
specimens.fact: Phacops often rolled up into a ball for protection, like a woodlouse, and many are found curled up that way.

specimens.name: Petoskey stone (fossil coral)
specimens.clue: A smooth, polished pebble covered in a pattern of six-sided cells.
specimens.fact: It's a fossil coral colony. Ice-age glaciers plucked pieces from the bedrock and ground them into pebbles, which collectors now hunt for in Michigan.

specimens.name: Sea scorpion (Eurypterus remipes)
specimens.clue: A scorpion-like creature with paddle-shaped legs and a long spiky tail.
specimens.fact: Eurypterus makes up more than 95% of all sea scorpion fossils ever found, and it is the state fossil of New York.

specimens.name: 'Dudley bug' trilobite (Calymene blumenbachii)
specimens.clue: A small trilobite with a big rounded head, lying on grey limestone.
specimens.fact: So many were found in the limestone quarries of Dudley that it appeared on the town's coat of arms, earning the nickname the 'Dudley bug'.

specimens.name: Isotelus (giant trilobite)
specimens.clue: A big, smooth, oval trilobite with faint segments, on pale stone.
specimens.fact: The state fossil of Ohio. Isotelus holds the record for the largest trilobite fossil ever found, at over 70 cm long.

specimens.name: Marrella splendens
specimens.clue: A tiny feathery creature with long sweeping spines, like a shadow on dark shale.
specimens.fact: The most common animal in the Burgess Shale: tens of thousands have been collected. A dark stain is often preserved around it.

specimens.name: Dickinsonia
specimens.clue: An oval imprint with fine ribs running out from a line down its middle.
specimens.fact: One of the oldest known animals, from before the Cambrian. It lived on shallow sea floors, feeding on mats of microbes.

specimens.name: Septarian nodule
specimens.clue: A smooth dark stone crossed by cracks filled with pale crystal, like a tortoise shell.
specimens.fact: Not a turtle or a dinosaur egg: it's a concretion, a lump of mineral that hardened inside mud. It cracked as it shrank, and the cracks later filled with crystal.

specimens.name: Moqui marbles
specimens.clue: Two dark, round balls, one cracked open to show sand inside.
specimens.fact: These iron-coated sandstone balls look like fossil eggs, but they formed when iron-rich groundwater flowed through the rock. They're named after a Hopi legend.

specimens.name: Fulgurite ('fossilised lightning')
specimens.clue: A rough, hollow tube of fused sand, like a stone branch or a fossil burrow.
specimens.fact: Made by lightning, not by life. When lightning strikes sand it can melt it into a glassy tube in a split second.

specimens.name: Atlantic horseshoe crab shell
specimens.clue: A helmet-shaped brown shell with a long spiked tail, lying on pebbles.
specimens.foundIn: A beach in Rhode Island, USA
specimens.fact: Horseshoe crabs are still alive today and look much like fossils of their ancient relatives. Despite the name, they're more closely related to spiders than to crabs.

specimens.name: Insects in copal
specimens.clue: A glowing orange lump with tiny bugs and bubbles trapped inside.
specimens.fact: Copal is tree resin that has hardened but hasn't had time to become amber. It's often sold as amber, but the insects inside aren't ancient.

specimens.name: Piltdown Man
specimens.clue: A human-like skull with a heavy, ape-like jaw.
specimens.fact: Presented in 1912 as a missing link between apes and humans. It was really a human skull and an orangutan jaw, stained to look old. The hoax was exposed in 1953.

specimens.name: Fairy stone (clay concretion)
specimens.clue: A flat, rounded grey stone with curving ridges, like a fossil shell.
specimens.fact: Not a shell: it's a concretion, a lump where minerals cemented clay together. In Sweden these odd shapes are called 'marlekor' and were once thought to be made by fairies.

specimens.name: Desert rose
specimens.clue: A pale ball of thin, curved blades, like a stone flower.
specimens.fact: Not a petrified flower: it's a cluster of flat gypsum crystals that grew in sand, trapping sand grains as they formed.

photo.author: Stephanie Clifford from Arlington, VA, USA

specimens.name: Pyrite sun
specimens.clue: A flat, golden metallic disc with lines radiating from its centre.
specimens.fact: It looks like a fossil sand dollar turned to gold, but it's a disc of pyrite crystals that grew outwards in a thin gap between layers of shale.

specimens.name: Liesegang rings in sandstone
specimens.clue: A sandstone boulder with wavy bands of colour, like the rings of a tree.
specimens.fact: Not petrified wood: these bands formed when mineral-rich water seeped through the rock and left colour behind in a repeating pattern.

specimens.name: Moss agate
specimens.clue: A polished white pebble with green, moss-like threads inside.
specimens.fact: The 'moss' isn't a plant: it's green minerals, mostly iron or manganese oxides, that grew in thread-like patterns inside the stone.

specimens.name: Ripple marks in sandstone
specimens.clue: A slab of red rock with neat, evenly spaced ridges.
specimens.fact: Ripples left by water nearly 2 billion years ago, long before animals existed. They're a record of moving water, not of life.

specimens.name: Tafoni (honeycomb weathering)
specimens.clue: A rock riddled with rounded holes, like a sponge or a coral.
specimens.foundIn: Bean Hollow State Beach, California, USA
specimens.fact: Not a fossil sponge or coral: these holes were hollowed out of the rock by weathering.

specimens.name: Thunder egg
specimens.clue: A rock cut in half to show a starburst of blue and white crystal inside.
specimens.fact: Thunder eggs form inside layers of volcanic ash. They look like ordinary rocks outside, but are filled with agate or quartz, not with anything that was once alive.

specimens.name: Chiastolite
specimens.clue: A slice of brownish stone with a dark cross through its centre.
specimens.fact: The cross is a natural pattern inside crystals of andalusite, a mineral. It was never alive.

specimens.name: Marcasite nodule
specimens.clue: A dark, knobbly lump, like a fossil sponge or a brain coral.
specimens.fact: Pure mineral: marcasite is a form of iron sulfide, like pyrite. It often crumbles over time because of its unstable crystal structure.

specimens.name: Modern sand dollar
specimens.clue: A flat, round disc covered in fine bristles, with a faint five-petal pattern.
specimens.fact: A modern sand dollar, a flat, burrowing kind of sea urchin. Its fossil relatives look very similar, but this one is from a museum collection of living species.

photo.author: Eric A. Lazo-Wasem, Yale Peabody Museum

specimens.name: Edible sea urchin shell
specimens.clue: A round, reddish shell covered in neat rows of tiny bumps.
specimens.fact: The empty shell of a modern edible sea urchin, with its spines gone. Fossil urchins, like the heart urchin Micraster, look much the same.

specimens.name: Moa leg bone
specimens.clue: A huge, dark brown leg bone from a bird, longer than a forearm.
specimens.fact: Moa were giant flightless birds, the largest about 3.6 m tall. They were hunted to extinction after people reached New Zealand around 1300, so their bones are only centuries old.

photo.author: Lukas Large from Stourbridge, United Kingdom

specimens.name: Dodo skeleton
specimens.clue: The skeleton of a plump, flightless bird with a big hooked beak.
specimens.fact: Dodos lived only on the island of Mauritius and died out in the late 1600s. Their bones are far too young to be fossils.

specimens.name: Coelacanth
specimens.clue: A large, chunky fish with fleshy, limb-like fins.
specimens.fact: Coelacanths were thought to have died out with the dinosaurs until a living one was caught in 1938. This one was caught in 1974.

specimens.name: Living stromatolites
specimens.clue: Dark, rounded rock-like mounds in shallow water along a beach.
specimens.foundIn: Hamelin Pool, Shark Bay, Western Australia
specimens.fact: These look like ancient rocks, and fossil stromatolites are some of the oldest signs of life. But these are alive, built layer by layer by microbes today.

specimens.name: Ram's horn squid shell
specimens.clue: A small, white, tightly coiled shell, about the size of a fingertip.
specimens.fact: The internal shell of Spirula, a deep-sea squid alive today. It looks like a tiny ammonite and often washes up on beaches.

specimens.name: Paper nautilus (argonaut) shell
specimens.clue: A delicate, cream-coloured coiled shell with fine ribs and a wavy edge.
specimens.fact: Made by a female argonaut, a kind of octopus, as a paper-thin case for her eggs. It looks like an ammonite, but it's modern and isn't even a true shell.

specimens.name: Cuttlebone
specimens.clue: A smooth, white, oval object lying on wet sand.
specimens.fact: The internal 'bone' of a modern cuttlefish. It washes up on beaches all the time and can look like a fossil, but the animal is alive today.

specimens.name: Lingula shell
specimens.clue: A long, shiny, greenish shell shaped like a tongue.
specimens.fact: Lingula is alive today, burrowing in sandy sea floors. It was long called a 'living fossil' because ancient shells of its relatives look so similar.

specimens.name: Crab moult
specimens.clue: An empty crab shell with a spiky front edge and a leopard-like pattern.
specimens.fact: The shell a lady crab shed as it grew. Crabs moult their whole outer skeleton, so beaches are full of empty shells like this one.

specimens.name: Carved fake trilobites
specimens.clue: A slab of pale rock with several neat trilobites on its surface.
specimens.fact: These 'trilobites' were carved into the rock and sold as fossils. Look-alike sets of identical, shallow trilobites are a warning sign.

specimens.name: Concrete 'dinosaur fossil'
specimens.clue: A reddish rock surface with a trilobite-like creature and three large round eggs.
specimens.foundIn: A public park in Dalian, China
specimens.fact: A 'fossil' made of concrete and glass fibre for a park display. Nothing here was ever alive.

specimens.name: 'Archaeoraptor'
specimens.clue: A cracked slab with a bird-like skeleton spread across several pieces.
specimens.fact: Announced in 1999 as a missing link between dinosaurs and birds. It was really pieces of different real fossils glued together; part of the tail came from a Microraptor.

specimens.name: The Cardiff Giant
specimens.clue: A huge stone figure of a man, lying on its back.
specimens.fact: Dug up in 1869 and shown as a 'petrified man', 3 metres tall. It was really a carved stone statue, and crowds paid to see it anyway.

photo.author: Martin Lewison from Forest Hills, NY, U.S.A.

specimens.name: Sideshow 'mermaid'
specimens.clue: A shrivelled creature with a monkey-like head and a scaly fish's tail.
specimens.fact: Fake mermaids drew paying crowds. The famous 'Fiji mermaid' shown by P. T. Barnum was a monkey sewn to a fish; this papier-mâché one is from the same collection.

specimens.name: Eozoön canadense
specimens.clue: A slab of rock with fine green and pale bands running through it.
specimens.fact: Once hailed as the oldest fossil animal ever found. It turned out to be layers of minerals, with no life involved at all.

specimens.name: Jenny Haniver
specimens.clue: A small, dried, winged creature with a face like a little demon.
specimens.fact: A dried skate or ray, cut and shaped to look like a demon or dragon. Sailors have made and sold these since the 1500s.

specimens.name: Woolly rhinoceros skull
specimens.clue: A long, heavy skull with a thick bony ridge along the top of the nose.
specimens.fact: Woolly rhinos were as big as today's white rhino, covered in thick hair for the cold steppes. Some have been found mummified in Siberian permafrost.

specimens.name: Mastodon tooth
specimens.clue: A chunky tooth with rows of rounded, cone-shaped bumps.
specimens.fact: Mastodons were relatives of elephants. Their teeth had pointed cones for chewing leaves and twigs, unlike the flat, ridged teeth of mammoths.

specimens.name: Diprotodon skull (giant wombat relative)
specimens.clue: A huge skull with two big front teeth sticking forward, like a giant rodent's.
specimens.fact: The largest marsupial that ever lived, about the size of a hippo. When its bones were first found in 1830, scientists guessed they came from rhinos, elephants or hippos.

specimens.name: Steppe bison skull
specimens.clue: A broad skull with two long, curving horns.
specimens.fact: Steppe bison roamed the cold grasslands from Western Europe to Alaska. This skull is about 40,000 years old.

specimens.name: Cave hyena skull
specimens.clue: A strong, short-snouted skull with big crushing teeth.
specimens.fact: Cave hyenas lived in Britain during the Ice Age and dragged hundreds of bones into their caves. This one is 22,000 to 40,000 years old.

specimens.name: Laetoli footprint
specimens.clue: A human-like footprint pressed into grey, gritty rock.
specimens.fact: Left by Australopithecus afarensis, Lucy's species, walking upright through fresh volcanic ash. Mary Leakey's team found the trackway in 1976.

photo.author: Ellison J. McNutt, Kevin G. Hatala, Catherine Miller, James Adams, Jesse Casana, Andrew S. Deane, Nathaniel J. Dominy, Kallisti Fabian, Luke D. Fannin, Stephen Gaughan, Simone V. Thompson, Rebeca Thornburg, Erin Marie Williams-Hatala, Brian Zimmer, Charles M. Musiba & Jeremy M. DeSilva

specimens.name: Three-toed horse skull (Hipparion)
specimens.clue: A long, horse-like skull on a dark background.
specimens.fact: Hipparion was a horse with three toes on each foot. It lived about 10 to 5 million years ago and ate mostly grass on open savannahs.

specimens.name: Deinotherium skull
specimens.clue: An elephant-like skull with tusks curving down and back from the lower jaw.
specimens.fact: A giant relative of elephants, some bigger than any elephant alive. Its tusks grew down from its lower jaw instead of out from its upper jaw.

specimens.name: Shovel-tusker jaw (Amebelodon)
specimens.clue: A long lower jaw ending in two broad, flat tusks, like a shovel.
specimens.fact: Amebelodon was an elephant relative whose lower tusks were flattened into a shovel shape.

specimens.name: Thylacosmilus skull
specimens.clue: A skull with huge sabre fangs and a bony flange on the jaw to protect them.
specimens.fact: It looks like a sabre-toothed cat, but it wasn't a cat at all. It was closely related to marsupials and evolved the same sabre teeth separately.

specimens.name: Ecphora snail
specimens.clue: A chunky spiral shell with broad, flared ribs, like a stack of plates.
specimens.fact: Ecphora was a predatory sea snail that lived along North America's east coast. It's the state fossil of Maryland.

specimens.name: Wasp in Dominican amber
specimens.clue: A clear golden pebble with a tiny wasp and an air bubble trapped inside.
specimens.fact: Dominican amber is the hardened resin of an extinct tree. It's almost always clear and holds more insects than Baltic amber.

specimens.name: 'Ida' (Darwinius masillae)
specimens.clue: A small, complete skeleton of a long-tailed animal with grasping hands.
specimens.fact: An early primate, distantly related to lemurs. It's one of the most complete fossil primates ever found.

photo.author: Jens L. Franzen, Philip D. Gingerich, Jörg Habersetzer1, Jørn H. Hurum, Wighart von Koenigswald, B. Holly Smith

specimens.name: Shark tooth (Otodus obliquus)
specimens.clue: A pale, pointed shark tooth with two small side points at its base.
specimens.fact: From a shark up to 9 metres long, thought to be an early ancestor of the famous megalodon.

specimens.name: Titanoboa vertebra
specimens.clue: A single dark backbone, about the size of a fist, on a museum stand.
specimens.fact: From the largest snake ever found, discovered in a Colombian coal mine. It lived not long after the dinosaurs died out.

specimens.name: Petrified redwood stump
specimens.clue: A giant tree stump turned to stone, standing in a forest clearing.
specimens.fact: A giant redwood buried by volcanic mudflows and turned to stone. The same lake beds hold beautifully preserved insects and leaves.

specimens.name: Brontothere skull
specimens.clue: A massive skull with a pair of blunt, forked horns on its nose.
specimens.fact: Brontotheres were rhino-sized relatives of horses. Hundreds of complete skulls have been found, making them one of the best-known large fossil mammals.

specimens.name: Mesohippus (early horse)
specimens.clue: A slender horse skeleton about the size of a greyhound, with three toes on each foot.
specimens.fact: An early horse only about 60 cm tall at the shoulder. It walked on three toes rather than a single hoof.

specimens.name: Oreodont skull (Merycoidodon)
specimens.clue: A short, rounded skull of a sheep-sized grazing animal, set in rock.
specimens.fact: Oreodonts were plant-eaters found only in North America. Their skulls are among the most common fossils in the Badlands.

specimens.name: Fossil palm frond
specimens.clue: A fan-shaped leaf the size of an umbrella, with two small fish beside it.
specimens.fact: Palms once grew in Wyoming, when its climate was much warmer. The lake mud that buried this leaf was laid down in yearly layers.

specimens.name: Triceratops brow horn
specimens.clue: A long, rough, tapering horn core, as long as an arm.
specimens.fact: Triceratops was one of the very last dinosaurs, living right up to the mass extinction 66 million years ago.

specimens.name: Oviraptor eggs
specimens.clue: A ring of long, dark grey eggs laid in a circle in reddish rock.
specimens.fact: Oviraptor means 'egg thief': the first one was found on a nest and thought to be stealing eggs. Embryos found in eggs like these show they were its own.

specimens.name: Duck-billed dinosaur skin impression
specimens.clue: A row of tail bones with a bumpy, pebbly texture pressed into the rock around them.
specimens.fact: Part of the tail of Edmontosaurus, a duck-billed dinosaur. The pattern around the bones is an impression of its scaly skin.

specimens.name: Mosasaurus jaw
specimens.clue: A long, heavy jaw with big cone-shaped teeth, lit up in a dark room.
specimens.fact: Not a dinosaur but a giant sea lizard. The first Mosasaurus skulls were found in chalk quarries near the Dutch city of Maastricht.

specimens.name: Pteranodon skull
specimens.clue: A very long, toothless, pointed beak with a backward-pointing crest.
specimens.fact: A flying reptile with a wingspan of over 6 metres. More Pteranodon fossils have been found than of any other pterosaur.

specimens.name: Confuciusornis (early bird)
specimens.clue: A crow-sized bird skeleton with long tail feathers, on a pale slab.
specimens.fact: One of the earliest birds with a toothless beak, like modern birds.

specimens.name: Sinosauropteryx
specimens.clue: A small two-legged skeleton with a long tail fringed by a dark, fluffy outline.
specimens.fact: Found in 1996, it was the first dinosaur outside the bird family found with feathers. Its fuzz even preserves a striped tail pattern.

specimens.name: Psittacosaurus skull
specimens.clue: A short, deep skull with a hooked, parrot-like beak.
specimens.fact: The 'parrot lizard'. With up to 13 species, it's the dinosaur genus with the most known species.

specimens.name: Borealopelta (armoured dinosaur)
specimens.clue: A dark, flattened body covered in armour plates and spikes, like a statue.
specimens.fact: Found by a miner in an oil-sands mine, this armoured dinosaur is so well preserved that its skin and armour are still in place.

specimens.name: Archaefructus (early flowering plant)
specimens.clue: Thin branching stems with small leaves, printed dark on grey rock.
specimens.fact: One of the earliest known flowering plants. It probably grew in water, a bit like a pond weed.

specimens.name: Baculites (straight ammonite)
specimens.clue: A shiny dark rod, like a piece of pipe, with a wavy pattern on its surface.
specimens.fact: An ammonite with an almost straight shell instead of a coil. It lived worldwide and briefly survived the extinction that ended the dinosaurs.

specimens.name: Belemnite (Belemnitella americana)
specimens.clue: Two dark, bullet-shaped stones, each about finger-length.
specimens.fact: The bullet-shaped 'guard' from inside a squid-like animal. Belemnitella americana is the state fossil of Delaware.

specimens.name: Inoceramus clam
specimens.clue: A pale, broad shell covered in deep concentric ridges.
specimens.fact: A relative of today's pearl oysters. Inoceramus lived from the Early Jurassic until the end of the Cretaceous.

specimens.name: Spinosaurus tooth
specimens.clue: A long, straight, cone-shaped tooth, brown and glossy at the tip.
specimens.fact: Spinosaurus had straight teeth for gripping fish. Its first fossils, found in Egypt, were destroyed in World War II.

specimens.name: Carcharodontosaurus tooth
specimens.clue: A large, curved, blade-like tooth with fine serrations, sitting in rock.
specimens.fact: Its name means 'shark-toothed lizard' after its blade-like teeth. It was first named from two teeth found in Algeria.

specimens.name: Fish and lobster from Lebanon
specimens.clue: A pale slab with a small fish and a long lobster-like creature side by side.
specimens.fact: Limestone quarries in Lebanon are famous for beautifully preserved fish, shrimp and lobsters from an ancient sea.

specimens.name: Pterodactylus
specimens.clue: A delicate skeleton with long wing fingers and a narrow beak, on smooth pale stone.
specimens.fact: The first pterosaur ever named and recognised as a flying reptile.

specimens.name: Horseshoe crab with its trackway
specimens.clue: A horseshoe crab at the end of a long trail of tiny footprints.
specimens.fact: This horseshoe crab left a trail of footprints before it died. It looks almost identical to horseshoe crabs alive today.

specimens.name: Aspidorhynchus fish
specimens.clue: A slender fish with a long, pointed snout, on pale limestone.
specimens.fact: A fast, long-snouted predatory fish, a bit like a modern garfish.

specimens.name: Sea lily (Seirocrinus)
specimens.clue: A huge feathery fan on a long stalk, spread out on dark stone.
specimens.fact: This sea lily hung upside down from floating driftwood. With stalks close to 30 metres long, it's the largest crinoid known.

specimens.name: Ichthyosaurus skull
specimens.clue: A long, narrow, toothy snout with a huge eye socket, set in dark rock.
specimens.fact: Ichthyosaurus was one of the first ichthyosaurs known to science, from the fossil-rich cliffs of the Dorset coast.

specimens.name: Sea lily (Pentacrinites)
specimens.clue: A dense, feathery fan of fine branches pressed flat in pale rock.
specimens.fact: A sea lily with star-shaped stem pieces. One rock layer at Lyme Regis is so full of them that it's called the Pentacrinites Bed.

specimens.name: Asteroceras ammonite
specimens.clue: A creamy, strongly ribbed coiled shell sitting on a dark rock base.
specimens.fact: A fast-swimming ammonite from the Frodingham Ironstone, rock that was mined for iron ore.

specimens.name: Complete belemnite (Passaloteuthis)
specimens.clue: A dark bullet-shaped point with a faint body and arms of tiny hooks fanning behind it.
specimens.fact: Usually only the bullet-shaped guard of a belemnite survives. This rare one keeps its soft body and its arms, lined with tiny hooks.

photo.author: Dominique Jenny, Dirk Fuchs, Alexander I. Arkhipkin, Rolf B. Hauff, Barbara Fritschi, Christian Klug

specimens.name: Megalosaurus jaws
specimens.clue: Pieces of an upper and lower jaw with big, curved, blade-like teeth.
specimens.fact: The only certain Megalosaurus fossils come from Oxfordshire. In 1824 it became the first dinosaur ever to be scientifically named.

photo.author: the paleobear from Lontananza, Loreto, Peru

specimens.name: Stegosaurus back plate
specimens.clue: A large, thin, flat plate of bone with a ridged surface, mounted on a wall.
specimens.fact: One of the kite-shaped plates that ran in two rows along a Stegosaurus's back.

specimens.name: Diplodocus tail bone
specimens.clue: A big, chunky backbone with a tall spine, longer than a forearm.
specimens.fact: From the tail of Diplodocus, a long-necked sauropod. Sauropods were the largest animals ever to walk on land.

specimens.name: Coelophysis skull
specimens.clue: A long, narrow skull with many small, sharp teeth, set in rock.
specimens.fact: One of the earliest dinosaurs, a slim, fast hunter. Hundreds were found buried together at Ghost Ranch in New Mexico.

specimens.name: Plateosaurus skeleton
specimens.clue: A pale skeleton with a long neck, a small head and strong hind legs.
specimens.fact: An early long-necked plant-eater, an early relative of later giants like Diplodocus.

specimens.name: Ceratites ammonoid
specimens.clue: A thick brown coiled shell with a wavy, zigzag pattern across it.
specimens.fact: A Triassic ammonoid. The zigzag lines show where its inner walls met the outer shell.

specimens.name: Lystrosaurus skull
specimens.clue: A rounded skull with a short snout and two small tusks, half buried in grey rock.
specimens.fact: A pig-sized plant-eater that survived the biggest mass extinction ever and then spread across the supercontinent Pangaea.

specimens.name: Mixosaurus (early ichthyosaur)
specimens.clue: A slim, dolphin-shaped reptile skeleton curled across a dark slab.
specimens.fact: One of the earlier ichthyosaurs, from a famous fossil site on the border of Italy and Switzerland.

specimens.name: Cynognathus skull
specimens.clue: A long, dog-like skull with big canine teeth.
specimens.fact: A predator closely related to mammals. Its fossils are found in Africa, South America and Antarctica, which were joined together at the time.

specimens.name: Chirotherium footprints
specimens.clue: A slab of sandstone with a line of hand-shaped footprints.
specimens.fact: These prints look like human hands, which puzzled early scientists. They were made by a relative of crocodiles walking across mud.

specimens.name: Glossopteris leaves
specimens.clue: A slab scattered with tongue-shaped leaves in shades of orange and brown.
specimens.fact: A seed plant whose leaves are found in South America, Africa, India, Australia and Antarctica: evidence those continents were once joined.

specimens.name: Helicoprion tooth whorl
specimens.clue: A spiral of pointed teeth, coiled like a circular saw blade, in orange rock.
specimens.fact: These spiral tooth whorls puzzled scientists for a century. They sat in the lower jaw of a shark-like fish.

specimens.name: Fusulinid limestone
specimens.clue: A rock surface packed with hundreds of tiny, rice-shaped grains.
specimens.fact: Each 'grain of rice' is the shell of a single-celled sea creature called a fusulinid.

specimens.name: Palaeoniscum fish
specimens.clue: A dark, scaly fish pressed flat in grey shale.
specimens.fact: An early ray-finned fish. Many are found in the copper-rich shale of central Germany.

specimens.name: Seymouria
specimens.clue: A sprawling four-legged skeleton with a broad head, on a pale slab.
specimens.fact: An amphibian so well suited to life on land that it was first thought to be an early reptile.

specimens.name: Calamites stem
specimens.clue: A stone cylinder with neat, straight ridges running along it, next to a coin.
specimens.fact: A piece of a giant horsetail that grew into trees 30 metres tall in coal swamps. Its small relatives still grow today.

specimens.name: Sigillaria bark
specimens.clue: Dark rock covered in neat vertical rows of rounded scars.
specimens.fact: Bark from a tree-like relative of quillworts, a cousin of the scale tree Lepidodendron.

specimens.name: Stigmaria (fossil tree root)
specimens.clue: A long, grey rock branch dotted with small round scars.
specimens.fact: Part of the root system of a giant coal-swamp tree like Sigillaria or Lepidodendron.

specimens.name: Annularia leaves
specimens.clue: Black star-shaped whorls of thin leaves on grey rock.
specimens.fact: These leaf whorls grew on Calamites, the giant tree-sized horsetails of the coal swamps.

specimens.name: Pecopteris fern
specimens.clue: A grey slab printed with fern fronds and their neat rows of leaflets.
specimens.fact: Leaves mostly from Psaronius, a tree fern of the coal swamps.

specimens.name: Essexella (fossil jellyfish)
specimens.clue: A brown oval stone nodule with a faint bell-shaped outline inside.
specimens.fact: A fossil jellyfish. It makes up 42% of all finds in part of the Mazon Creek fossil beds.

specimens.name: Productid brachiopod
specimens.clue: A pale, ribbed shell set in black flint and brown limestone.
specimens.fact: Productids were the most common brachiopods of the Permian, then almost all died out in the great extinction.

specimens.name: Crinoid stems in limestone
specimens.clue: A lump of grey limestone with pale, segmented stems running through it.
specimens.fact: Bits of sea lily stems. Some limestones are made almost entirely of crinoid pieces.

specimens.name: Lithostrotion coral
specimens.clue: A lumpy rock packed with small round tubes, like a bundle of straws.
specimens.fact: A colonial coral that is common in Carboniferous Limestone.

specimens.name: Goniatites
specimens.clue: Two small, dark, rounded coiled shells beside a pale stone ring.
specimens.fact: Early ammonoids with zigzag lines on their shells.

specimens.name: Archimedes bryozoan
specimens.clue: A corkscrew-shaped twist running through a rock covered in fine lacy mesh.
specimens.fact: The 'screw' was the central support of a colony of tiny animals that built a lacy spiral net around it.

specimens.name: Bothriolepis (armoured fish)
specimens.clue: A small boxy fish with armour plates and jointed, arm-like fins.
specimens.fact: One of the most common armoured fish of its time. Its fins were encased in bony tubes, like arms in armour.

specimens.name: Eusthenopteron
specimens.clue: A dark fish shape with fleshy fins, pressed into an oval stone.
specimens.fact: A lobe-finned fish whose fin bones match the arm bones of land animals, which made it famous in the story of how fish moved onto land.

specimens.name: Pterichthyodes ('winged fish')
specimens.clue: A flat, armoured fish with two stiff, wing-like fins.
specimens.fact: Its fossils are common in Scotland's Old Red Sandstone, and were among the first recognised for what they were.

specimens.name: Archaeopteris (early tree)
specimens.clue: A grey slab with faint, fern-like branches running across it.
specimens.fact: One of the first trees with woody trunks like modern trees, though it reproduced with spores.

specimens.name: Rhynie chert
specimens.clue: A hard, banded grey and yellow rock with tiny tube shapes inside.
specimens.fact: This rock preserves some of the earliest land plants and animals in amazing detail, right down to their cells.

specimens.name: Gilboa fossil tree stumps
specimens.clue: Grey stone tree stumps set out on a lawn beside a forest.
specimens.fact: Stumps from one of the world's oldest known forests. A 2005 find showed what the complete trees looked like.

specimens.name: Brittle star in slate
specimens.clue: A star with five long, thin, wavy arms, glinting on dark grey slate.
specimens.fact: The Hunsrück Slate is famous for animals preserved in shiny pyrite, sometimes with fine soft parts.

specimens.name: Agoniatites
specimens.clue: A metallic, coiled shell set into a block of pale rock.
specimens.fact: One of the earliest ammonoids, the group that later gave rise to ammonites.

specimens.name: Chain coral (Halysites)
specimens.clue: A dome of rock covered in a wiggly, chain-like mesh.
specimens.fact: A colonial coral whose tubes join up into chains when seen from above.

specimens.name: Cooksonia (early land plant)
specimens.clue: A tiny Y-shaped plant stem with knobs at its tips, faint on grey rock.
specimens.fact: One of the oldest known land plants: a few centimetres tall, with no leaves or roots.

specimens.name: Pentamerus brachiopod
specimens.clue: A big, rounded pale lump with a single groove down the middle.
specimens.fact: This is an internal mould: the shell dissolved away, leaving a cast of its inside.

specimens.name: Monograptus graptolites
specimens.clue: Dark rock covered in criss-crossing thin pale lines, like scratches.
specimens.fact: Each line was a colony of tiny animals that drifted in the ocean. Graptolites are used to date rocks.

specimens.name: Dalmanites trilobite
specimens.clue: A neat trilobite with a long pointed tail spine, on grey rock.
specimens.fact: A trilobite named after the Swedish naturalist Johan Wilhelm Dalman.

specimens.name: Honeycomb coral (Favosites)
specimens.clue: A pale rock made of tightly packed, many-sided cells, like a honeycomb.
specimens.fact: A colonial coral whose tube walls had tiny pores linking neighbouring animals.

specimens.name: Stalk-eyed trilobite (Asaphus kowalewskii)
specimens.clue: A trilobite with two long eye stalks sticking up like a snail's.
specimens.fact: Its eyes sat on long stalks, perhaps so it could peek out while buried in the sea floor.

specimens.name: 'Tuning fork' graptolite (Didymograptus)
specimens.clue: Pale, saw-edged strips lying across dark slate.
specimens.fact: A floating colony of tiny animals. Graptolites changed so fast that geologists use them to date rocks.

specimens.name: Flexicalymene trilobite
specimens.clue: A chunky, ridged trilobite, partly rolled up.
specimens.fact: Like many trilobites, Flexicalymene could roll up for protection. It's often found curled up.

specimens.name: Echinosphaerites (cystoid)
specimens.clue: A handful of small, round, yellowish stone balls.
specimens.fact: Not marbles: these are cystoids, round relatives of sea urchins that sat on the sea floor.

specimens.name: Ogygiocarella trilobite
specimens.clue: A large, flat, oval trilobite printed on grey slate.
specimens.fact: A flat trilobite that was once common in the seas covering what is now Wales.

specimens.name: Receptaculites
specimens.clue: A rock surface with a spiral pattern of tiny cells, like a sunflower head, beside a coin.
specimens.fact: Nicknamed the 'sunflower coral', though it wasn't a coral. What it really was is still debated.

photo.author: Mark A. Wilson (Department of Geology, The College of Wooster)

specimens.name: Anomalocaris grasping arm
specimens.clue: A curved, segmented limb with spikes along its underside, on brown shale.
specimens.fact: One of the grasping arms of Anomalocaris, a large hunter of Cambrian seas. Arms like this were once mistaken for shrimp.

specimens.name: Opabinia
specimens.clue: A small segmented creature with flaps along its sides, on grey shale.
specimens.fact: A strange animal with five eyes and a long nozzle ending in a claw. When first shown at a meeting, it made the audience laugh.

specimens.name: Hallucigenia
specimens.clue: A tiny worm-like creature with a row of long spines along one side.
specimens.fact: So odd that it was first reconstructed upside down, walking on its spines.

specimens.name: Pikaia
specimens.clue: A small, flat, curved ribbon of a creature on grey shale.
specimens.fact: An early chordate, part of the wider group that includes all animals with backbones.

specimens.name: Paradoxides trilobite
specimens.clue: A large trilobite with long spines along its sides.
specimens.fact: A large trilobite found around the world. One record specimen is 37 cm long.

specimens.name: Olenellus trilobite
specimens.clue: A trilobite with a big half-moon head and long curved spines.
specimens.fact: One of the early trilobites, from the time when animals with hard shells first became common.

specimens.name: Redlichia trilobite
specimens.clue: A flat trilobite with spiny cheeks, on a square block of dark rock.
specimens.fact: One of the early trilobites, known from China and Australia.

specimens.name: Archaeocyath
specimens.clue: A pale, cup-shaped outline in black rock.
specimens.fact: A sponge that built some of the first reefs, then disappeared before the end of the Cambrian.

specimens.name: Retifacies (Chengjiang arthropod)
specimens.clue: A creature with many segments and a broad rounded head, faint on yellow stone.
specimens.fact: From the Chengjiang fossils of China, which preserve soft-bodied animals from the early Cambrian.

specimens.name: Spriggina
specimens.clue: A small segmented creature with a horseshoe-shaped head, printed on sandstone.
specimens.fact: One of the earliest animals, from before the Cambrian. It's the official fossil emblem of South Australia, and has been found nowhere else.

specimens.name: Kimberella
specimens.clue: A small oval imprint with a frilly edge, on pale rock.
specimens.fact: A slug-like animal that grazed on microbial mats, scraping them up with its mouth.

specimens.name: Cloudina
specimens.clue: A pale rock speckled with tiny dark tubes, like grains of rice.
specimens.fact: One of the first animals to build a hard shell: tiny stacks of cones. It died out at the start of the Cambrian.
